newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says satisfied with EU stability pact deal.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says satisfied with EU stability pact deal.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Monday said he was satisfied with the stability pact struck at last weekend's European Union summit in Dublin to underpin the solidity of the planned euro currency.

But, he said, political discretion in allowing states in recession to exceed the Maastricht treaty's fiscal criteria without being penalised must not undermine the independence of the planned European central bank.
Waigel said a so-called stability council, in which countries taking part in monetary union were represented should have only advisory and not decision-making powers.
"This should not act as a counterweight to the European central bank," Waigel told reporters after a meeting of his Christian Social Union (CSU) party in Munich.

Agreement on the stability pact helped the EU clear an important hurdle towards launching the single currency in 1999. Countries wanting to take part then need to ensure their state finances meet the Maastricht limits next year.

Leaders agreed in Dublin to exempt from automatic fines any country which overshoots the Maastricht deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product if its economy shrinks by more than two percent in a given year.
Waigel also gave in to pressure from other EU states to allow countries whose output shrinks by over 0.75 percent to plead "exceptional circumstances" to get off the fines.
He called the summit result "very satisfactory", and added that if negotiations on the stability pact had dragged on, problems could have arisen on foreign exchange markets.

Waigel, who in the runup to the Dublin summit had appeared isolated in pursuing his hard line on stability, said that he had received crucial backing at the talks from other so-called "hard currency" states in Europe.
And he played down differences between Bonn and Paris over the amount of political leeway allowed in enforcing the pact.
"If Germany and France work together, that brings the decisive breakthrough," he told reporters, adding, "we have no differences over fulfilling the (Maastricht) criteria."
